t58c_p5a: Your little one might ask what everybody wants to know: "But what if it doesn't work out?" The Guide doesn't have to know that to answer. "I don't know yet. Let's get your shoes on." It picks the next step that makes sense and fits what you care about, and the rest can stay unknown for a while.
t58c_p5b: I think a lot of us wait to feel sure before we do anything, which can mean waiting forever. The Guide doesn't need certainty. It's more like a parent on moving day who has no idea how the new school will go, but knows the boxes need labels: the next sensible thing, the one that fits what you care about, while the rest stays a mystery.
t58c_p5c: The Guide doesn't need to know how it all turns out before it does anything. Nobody gets to know that. It just looks for the next step that makes sense and fits what you care about. Sometimes that's a big one, like leaving a job, and sometimes it's putting the kettle on and calling your sister back.
t58c_p6a: Then there are the problems you can't move yet, however much you want to. Maybe the new job can't start until the background check clears. Your little one might hear the old parent in your head calling that lazy. How would you even be lazy at a background check? Waiting on something that's out of your hands isn't laziness, and it isn't avoiding anything. The Guide keeps track of what you're waiting for and what would open things up again, without pretending the check doesn't matter. Meanwhile, there's usually something else you can do.
t58c_p6b: Some problems are stuck on something outside you: a part on back order, a signature you're waiting for. I'd treat those differently from the ones you could do something about today. You're not being lazy by waiting on them, so there's no need to invent some heroic workaround that pretends the part isn't missing. Just keep in mind what you're waiting for and what would let you move again, and go do something else useful till then.
t58c_p6c: You might be waiting on a part for the car, or on somebody's signature. That kind of waiting isn't failing. It's just where things are, and no amount of willpower makes the part show up sooner, so I wouldn't go looking for a trick that pretends it will. Keep an eye on what you're waiting for, and on what would get it moving, and meanwhile do something else that can move.
t58c_p7a: Usually there's more than one thing going on, too, and one being stuck doesn't mean everything is. Your little one can still have a picnic while the car's in the shop. To pick what gets your attention today, I'd go by what you want most and what can actually move, unless something can't wait. And when everything feels like one big knot, try saying it in a single sentence, then choose one next step. Only stop to figure something out if the answer would change that step.
t58c_p7b: One stuck problem doesn't have to stop the rest of your life. I'd ask which of the others you can do something about, and which would help most with what you're going for, and start there, unless something else can't wait. When it all feels like too much, I'd try just one sentence about what's going on and one next step. The rest can wait unless the answer would change that step.
t58c_p7c: If you've got a few things going wrong at once, you don't have to solve them in order. The stuck one can sit while you deal with the one that can move. I'd go with whatever matters most for what you're trying to do and can happen today, unless something's due. And if it's all a jumble, one sentence about it and one next step is enough to get going. Anything else can wait, unless knowing it would change that step.
